img.author: CDC
img.alt: A fuzzy, round black-and-yellow insect with dark wings.

items.why: A bumblebee: round, fuzzy and striped black and yellow.
items.pearl: In Australia, bumblebees live wild only in Tasmania, where they arrived in the 1990s.

img.author: CDC/ Christine Prue
img.alt: A small spotted brown frog with webbed feet clinging to green and red plastic.

items.why: An African dwarf frog, a tiny frog that lives its whole life underwater.
items.pearl: It has no tongue. It shovels food into its mouth with its hands.

items.context: Out on the desert gravel at night.

img.author: CDC/ Mr. Graham Heid
img.alt: A long, flat, orange-brown segmented creature with many legs on gravel.

items.why: A centipede, with one pair of legs per body segment.
items.pearl: Centipedes always have an odd number of leg pairs, so none has exactly 100 legs.

items.context: Lives in quiet corners and old boxes.

img.author: CDC/ Dr. J. L. Conrad
img.alt: A long-legged light brown spider with a darker mark on its front half.

items.why: A brown recluse, with the violin-shaped mark on its front body.
items.pearl: Most spiders have eight eyes; the brown recluse has six, arranged in pairs.

items.context: Very close up. Sometimes found in old mattresses.

img.author: CDC/ CDC-DPDx; Blaine Mathison
img.alt: A shiny reddish-brown flat body with short antennae, seen very close.

items.why: A bed bug: flat, reddish-brown and oval.
items.pearl: Bed bugs can go months between meals, which makes them hard to starve out.

img.author: CDC/ Fenley (cropped)
img.alt: A pile of small, dark, wrinkled pieces of dried fruit in a white scoop.

items.why: Raisins: dried grapes, all wrinkles and sugar.
items.pearl: Drop raisins into fizzy drink and they 'dance' as bubbles lift them up and then pop at the surface.

items.context: Very close up and staring right back.

img.author: CDC/ Harold George Scott, PhD (cropped)
img.alt: A dark, shiny head covered in large plates with a round eye.

items.why: A coachwhip snake's head, with big smooth scales and a lidless eye.
items.pearl: Snakes have no eyelids. A clear scale covers each eye and is shed with the skin.

items.context: Face to face, very close up.

img.author: CDC
img.alt: A close insect face with two big dark eyes, three tiny eyes between them and two broken antennae.

items.why: A wasp's face: two big compound eyes and three tiny simple eyes in a triangle.
items.pearl: Those three little eyes, called ocelli, sense light and help with steady flight.

items.context: Electron microscope view of the underside, about 22 times life size.

img.author: CDC/ Janice Haney Carr (cropped)
img.alt: A grey electron microscope image of body segments, each with pairs of jointed legs.

items.why: A millipede's underside, with two pairs of legs on each segment.
items.pearl: For years no millipede had 1,000 legs. Then in 2021, one found deep underground in Western Australia turned out to have 1,306.

items.context: About 26 times life size, on a paddle left in water.

img.author: CDC/ Dr. Pratt (cropped)
img.alt: Many tiny dark, oval, textured objects packed together on a fibrous pale surface.

items.why: Aedes mosquito eggs laid on a damp paddle.
items.pearl: These eggs can survive dried out for months and hatch when rain floods them. Tip out water from pots and buckets.
